source.title: Silenced Biases: The Dark Side LLMs Learned to Refuse
source.authors: Rom Himelstein; Amit Levi; Brit Youngmann; Yaniv Nemcovsky; Avi Mendelson

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices. Some figures and heatmaps are flattened or not numerically legible in the text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests refusal bypass on sensitive QA prompts using activation steering and universal adversarial suffixes, methods different from the fine-tuning and token-position tests in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal-steering response success on SBB prompts, plus jailbreak-attack ASR heatmaps. The refusal-steering results are not tests of the claim versions as specified: steering alters activations rather than getting past an opening token. The suffix-attack ASR bears on V4, but its values are presented only in heatmaps; the text states only that the two attack runs had similar ASRs. Figure-only preference and fairness results are not refusal-rate results and are not included.
record.test_reason: This is a fairness study. It uses refusal-direction activation steering (Arditi et al.) as its own tool to get answers to sensitive bias QA prompts, and reports that tool's success rate. Activation steering is neither one of V4's opening, suffix or decoding methods nor weight localization (V5). The one V4-type operation, a GCG universal suffix, is used only to argue that jailbreaks induce bias. Its ASR appears only in Figure 12 heatmaps, with no numbers in the text. No version gets a readable result.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Authors conclude that alignment-induced refusals mask 'silenced' biases still encoded in activations. They argue that refusal steering exposes these biases without introducing new bias, whereas universal jailbreak suffixes induce their own, run-dependent bias patterns. They also find no clear link between model family, version or size and fairness.
record.recipe_differences: Uses refusal-direction activation ablation/subtraction and universal adversarial suffixes on sensitive fairness QA prompts; does not fine-tune models or measure token-position KL.
record.method_sensitivity: ASR differs substantially across models and without versus with refusal steering. The paper also reports run-to-run differences in jailbreak-induced DPD patterns, while stating that the two runs have similar ASRs.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating or subtracting a single refusal activation direction raises valid-answer rate on SBB sensitive-bias prompts from 12.85–92.25% to 94.33–100% across 10 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal on sensitive prompts is mediated by an activation direction whose removal near-eliminates refusal (refusal-direction claim, not token-depth).

fits_no_version.finding: On BBQ ambiguous questions for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, steering cuts refusal from 73% to 69%. With the refusal option removed, it cuts refusal from 69% to 37%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation steering only partly removes refusal when an explicit 'unknown' option is available.

record.problems: ASR values for the suffix-attack runs are only in heatmaps and cannot be reliably extracted from the supplied text. The study’s main response-success measure is on its SBB sensitive-bias QA prompts, not a standard harmful-request compliance test.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 6 and 11 show jailbreak-run DPD differences, but these are demographic preference-distribution results rather than refusal or compliance rates. Other figure-only fairness, KL, and activation-clustering results do not measure a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No per-token KL between aligned and base models. The KL here is over demographic answer distributions.
No prefilling or decoding attacks. The universal suffix ASR exists only as unreadable heatmaps, with no unattacked baseline reported alongside.
No weight or rank localization. A refusal direction in activations is used as a tool.

missing.what: BBQ refusal rates with and without refusal steering (73%→69%; with no refusal option, 69%→37%), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. The record's relation 'tests'/T2 is too generous. The only V4-type result (GCG suffix ASR) cannot be read, and the main results are the study's own activation-steering tool. Rows r1–r10 were marked 'partial' wherever the baseline was high. Their steered values are all ≥94%, so 'observed' fits better, though they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful-example fine-tuning and its effect on harmful-request compliance.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful-request compliance.
Per-token KL divergence between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.

The paper applies universal adversarial suffixes and reports ASR heatmaps on SBB sensitive-bias QA prompts, but the numerical success rates are not extractable from the text. It does not test compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes. Activation steering is also tested, but it changes internal activations rather than getting past response-opening tokens.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether the data or training objective produces shallow safety.
Training to spread safety beyond the first tokens and whether it holds up.
